correctness.rationale: Writing c=a+bk/v, the centered symbol b(B−(k/v)J) has a Schur factorization with row-factor length sqrt((v−1)/v) and column-factor length |b| sqrt(k(v−k)/v). The tensor-diagonal implementation gives their product as an operator-norm bound; adding the constant symbol contributes |c|. This covers c=0 and b=0 directly. The dual test with the conjugate polar partial isometry and normalized constant vectors gives the rectangular nuclear lower bound. In a complete incidence system, or a nontrivial 2-design, the replication and intersection counts give BB*= (r−λ)I+λJ, with r−λ=nk(v−k)/(v(v−1)). Centering splits the constant and orthogonal directions, so the singular values are sqrt(vn)|c| and |b|sqrt(r−λ) with multiplicity v−1, attaining the uniform bound in a finite width. The complete singleton design covers k=1. Over the reals the factors and witnesses are real when a,b are real. For balanced signs the Frobenius upper bound forces n≥v−1; deleting the constant column of a normalized real Hadamard gives balanced orthogonal columns and attains the minimum when such a matrix exists, not at every even v by assertion. Substitution and expansion give the two specializations and the fixed-k sparse limit. Independently checked 105 constant-vector polar witnesses, including genuinely complex coefficients and zero components (python /workspace/branches/independent_math_checks.py, section 1). These checks are finite, and the supplied verifier was inspected, not run.

evidence: Theorem 4.5 gives ||S_T||=Tr|T|/dim(T) for every complex square T with constant diagonals of |T| and |T*|; the lower-bound proof there uses the conjugate polar witness. Holbrook–Johnston–Schoch already states the unrestricted rectangular sign upper bound sqrt(min(v,n)).
broader_coverage.reasoning: The flat-polar criterion applies to a much broader class than two-level symbols and yields exact equality on the repeated square pencil. The sign-width obstruction is the previously known rectangular bound specialized to the balanced target; the Hadamard example then uses its orthogonal balanced columns. The idempotent norm gaps don't by themselves imply the pencil result.

evidence: For T=M⊗J_{Nt,vt}, the nonzero singular values are those of M multiplied by t sqrt(vN), so the Mathias norm is ||M||_*/sqrt(vN), independent of t. Applying the already-known polar-vector test to M itself attains this number: pair S_M(conj Q) with unit constant vectors to get ||M||_*/sqrt(vN). The elementary incidence Gram spectrum then gives exactly the claimed expression.

For a 2-design, the same flat diagonals hold even without transitive automorphisms: on the row side the constant/orthogonal spectral projections have constant diagonals, and on the column side the projections onto 1 and the centered row span have constant diagonals. The latter projection is F*F/(r−λ), where F=B−(k/v)J; its diagonal is constant by the common column norm. The coefficients of either projection can vanish without invalidating the criterion.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Apply the older equality theorem to the scaled-size replicas, then compress any admissible symbol into one of them. The normalized nuclear norm and its equality on a complete incidence support (also on the specified designs) are obtained by direct singular-value substitution. No new extremal upper bound or unknown equality construction is needed; specializations and the sparse expansion are immediate from that value.

evidence: For full incidence pencil M with dimensions v×N and t≥1, T=M⊗J_{Nt,vt} is square; independent permutations of repeated copies and the simultaneous underlying S_v actions are transitive on each index set. Thus both |T| and |T*| have constant diagonal, exactly the hypothesis in Mathias's theorem.

Every finite constant-k symbol with the same v,a,b is a rectangular submatrix of T for sufficiently large t: choose one row for each row type and distinct copies of every requested column, including repeated columns.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: Compression onto arbitrary specified row and column coordinates cannot increase the Schur multiplier norm, by extending an input matrix by zeros. Therefore the arbitrary-width problem is precisely the replicated complete pencil problem; repetition of columns poses no extra optimization.

originality.rationale: The explicit universal maximum is a direct corollary of the pre-existing Mathias exact Schur norm theorem, not just an application of a generic upper bound. The complete incidence pencil has transitive symmetries on both index sets and every allowed symbol is a submatrix of its sufficiently repeated replication. Squaring by replication lets the square Mathias theorem evaluate the sharp bound without the frozen record's centered inequality. Its polar witness is the same trace lower bound that attains it on the complete pencil. This is verified implication of the central claim, not a title match or a claim that the prior paper prints the same formula.
residual_risks: This independently verifies coverage by the classical exact theorem; it does not determine who first wrote out the fixed-weight expression or the rectangular application.

value.rationale: The prespecified weight constraint is natural and the formula is useful, but the underlying exact optimization is already determined by the classical flat-polar norm theorem and the direct complete-incidence compression. The incidence spectrum, sign asymptotic, and width consequence are routine once that reduction is made. The frozen record does not identify an additional new equality classification or fixed-width extremum that would constitute a distinct valuable result.
